answer: Voting weight is granted only to a key that holds one reserved uplink, called a harbor, prepaid with an ember of non-transferable bandwidth credits. At unpredictable gale probes the network demands a low-latency signed echo through that exact harbor. A late reply, a path that serves two keys, or an ember spent twice burns the residual credits and releases the harbor. To operate N identities, an attacker must buy N independent uplinks, lock N ember balances, and answer every gale from N distinct paths, so transit fees, locked credits, and always-on connectivity all scale with farm size.
